title: UNIT 6: SOLUTIONS TO ENVIRONMENTAL AND SUSTAINABILITY PROBLEMS
notes:
Environmental sustainability → the responsible use and management of natural resources so that present needs are met without reducing the ability of future generations to meet their needs.

Sustainable development → development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

Environmental problems → harmful changes in the natural environment caused by human activities, natural processes, or a combination of both.

title: 6.1 ENVIRONMENTAL PROBLEMS
notes:
Environmental problems → conditions that damage natural resources, ecosystems, human health, and the quality of life.

◆ MAJOR ENVIRONMENTAL PROBLEMS
✓ Deforestation → the removal or destruction of forests, often for agriculture, settlement, fuelwood and other activities.
✓ Soil degradation → decline in soil quality and productivity caused by erosion, nutrient depletion, overgrazing and inappropriate land use.
✓ Desertification → degradation of land in dry areas resulting from climatic variations and human activities.
✓ Water pollution → contamination of rivers, lakes, groundwater and other water bodies by harmful substances.
✓ Air pollution → contamination of the atmosphere by harmful gases, smoke, dust and other pollutants.
✓ Climate change → long-term changes in temperature and weather patterns, largely influenced in recent times by human emissions of greenhouse gases.
✓ Loss of biodiversity → reduction in the variety of plants, animals and other living organisms.
✓ Waste accumulation → increasing amounts of solid, liquid and hazardous waste that are not properly managed.
✓ Land degradation → deterioration of the physical, chemical and biological quality of land.

◆ ENVIRONMENTAL PROBLEMS AT DIFFERENT SCALES
✓ Local scale → problems affecting a community or small area, such as improper waste disposal, local water pollution and soil erosion.
✓ National scale → problems affecting large parts of a country, such as deforestation, land degradation and widespread pollution.
✓ Global scale → problems whose effects extend across national boundaries, such as climate change, biodiversity loss and ocean pollution.

◆ HUMAN IMPACTS ON THE NATURAL ENVIRONMENT
✓ Population growth increases demand for land, water, food, energy and other resources.
✓ Deforestation destroys habitats and reduces forest resources.
✓ Intensive agriculture can cause soil degradation and water pollution.
✓ Industrial activities can release pollutants into air, water and soil.
✓ Mining can disturb land and ecosystems.
✓ Urbanization changes natural landscapes and increases waste and resource consumption.
✓ Burning fossil fuels releases greenhouse gases and contributes to climate change.

◆ ECOLOGICAL FOOTPRINT
Ecological footprint → a measure of the amount of biologically productive land and water needed to provide the resources a population consumes and absorb the wastes it generates.

A large ecological footprint indicates high pressure on the Earth's productive ecosystems.

◆ ENVIRONMENTAL DEGRADATION
Environmental degradation → deterioration of the natural environment through the depletion of resources, destruction of ecosystems and pollution.

Environmental degradation can reduce agricultural productivity, threaten biodiversity, increase health problems and make sustainable development more difficult.

title: 6.2 THE SUSTAINABILITY CHALLENGE
notes:
Sustainability challenge → the difficulty of meeting the growing needs of present populations while maintaining the natural systems and resources required by present and future generations.

◆ CURRENT UNSUSTAINABILITY
✓ Rapid population growth increases demand for food, water, energy, housing and other resources.
✓ Increasing consumption puts greater pressure on natural resources.
✓ Unsustainable agricultural practices can reduce soil fertility and degrade land.
✓ Dependence on fossil fuels contributes to greenhouse gas emissions and climate change.
✓ Poor waste management causes pollution and health problems.
✓ Overuse of forests, fisheries, water and other resources can reduce their ability to recover.

◆ CARRYING CAPACITY AND BIOCAPACITY
Carrying capacity → the maximum population size that an environment can support over a long period without causing serious environmental degradation.

Biocapacity → the capacity of biologically productive ecosystems to regenerate renewable biological resources and absorb certain wastes, especially carbon dioxide.

When human demand for resources and ecological services exceeds the Earth's available biocapacity, ecological pressure increases and development becomes less sustainable.

◆ CORE STRATEGIES FOR SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT
✓ Climate change mitigation → actions that reduce greenhouse gas emissions or increase the removal of greenhouse gases from the atmosphere.
✓ Renewable energy → using naturally replenished energy sources such as solar, wind, hydropower and geothermal energy.
✓ Energy efficiency → reducing energy consumption while maintaining useful services and production.
✓ Sustainable agriculture → farming methods that maintain soil fertility, conserve water, protect biodiversity and support long-term agricultural production.
✓ Afforestation and reforestation → planting trees and restoring forests to protect soil, biodiversity and water resources.
✓ Proper waste management → reducing waste generation and applying reuse, recycling, composting and safe disposal.
✓ Water conservation → using water efficiently and protecting water sources from pollution and degradation.
✓ Sustainable resource use → using natural resources at rates that allow them to regenerate and remain available in the future.
✓ Environmental planning → considering environmental impacts when making development decisions.

title: 6.3 ROLE OF ENVIRONMENTAL EDUCATION AND MOVEMENTS
notes:
Environmental education → a process of developing knowledge, awareness, attitudes, skills and participation needed to understand environmental problems and take responsible action to protect the environment.

◆ IMPORTANCE OF ENVIRONMENTAL EDUCATION
✓ Creates awareness about environmental problems.
✓ Develops responsible attitudes toward natural resources.
✓ Encourages conservation of forests, soil, water and biodiversity.
✓ Helps people understand the causes and effects of environmental degradation.
✓ Promotes environmentally responsible behaviour.
✓ Encourages community participation in environmental protection.
✓ Supports sustainable development.

◆ ENVIRONMENTAL MOVEMENTS
Environmental movement → organized efforts by individuals, communities, organizations and governments to protect the environment and promote sustainable use of natural resources.

Environmental movements developed as awareness increased about pollution, resource depletion, habitat destruction and other environmental problems. Modern environmental movements expanded particularly during the twentieth century and increasingly addressed global issues such as climate change, biodiversity loss and sustainable development.

◆ MAJOR AREAS OF ENVIRONMENTAL MOVEMENTS
✓ Forest and wildlife conservation.
✓ Pollution control.
✓ Climate action.
✓ Protection of biodiversity.
✓ Sustainable use of natural resources.
✓ Environmental justice.
✓ Waste reduction and recycling.
✓ Protection of water resources.

◆ ROLE OF GOVERNMENTS
✓ Develop and enforce environmental laws and regulations.
✓ Establish protected areas and conservation programmes.
✓ Promote sustainable land and resource management.
✓ Control pollution and waste disposal.
✓ Support environmental education and research.
✓ Invest in renewable energy and environmentally friendly technologies.
✓ Cooperate with other countries on global environmental problems.

◆ ROLE OF INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS
✓ Promote international environmental cooperation.
✓ Support environmental research, education and conservation programmes.
✓ Provide technical and financial assistance to countries.
✓ Help develop international environmental agreements and policies.
✓ Encourage countries to work together on problems that cross national borders.

◆ ROLE OF INDIVIDUALS AND COMMUNITIES
✓ Use natural resources responsibly.
✓ Reduce, reuse and recycle materials.
✓ Avoid unnecessary pollution.
✓ Conserve water and energy.
✓ Plant and protect trees.
✓ Participate in community conservation activities.
✓ Follow environmental laws and regulations.
✓ Educate others about environmental protection.

Environmental stewardship → responsible care and management of the natural environment by governments, organizations, communities and individuals.

title: 6.4 ENVIRONMENTALLY FRIENDLY INDIGENOUS PRACTICES
notes:
Indigenous environmental knowledge → knowledge, skills, values and practices developed by local and indigenous communities through long-term interaction with their natural environment.

Traditional conservation practices → methods used by communities to protect natural resources, maintain ecological balance and support livelihoods.

◆ EXAMPLES OF ENVIRONMENTALLY FRIENDLY INDIGENOUS PRACTICES
✓ Traditional agroforestry → growing trees together with crops or livestock to conserve soil, provide resources and improve land productivity.
✓ Terracing and soil conservation → using traditional land-management methods to reduce soil erosion and conserve water.
✓ Crop diversification → growing different crops to reduce risks and maintain soil and ecosystem health.
✓ Traditional water conservation → protecting springs, wetlands and other water sources and using water carefully.
✓ Community-based forest protection → managing forests collectively and restricting destructive activities.
✓ Traditional grazing management → controlling livestock movement and grazing areas to prevent overgrazing.
✓ Protection of sacred natural sites → conserving forests, trees, water sources or other places considered culturally or spiritually important.
✓ Use of locally adapted crops and livestock → maintaining species and varieties suited to local environmental conditions.
✓ Traditional weather and ecological knowledge → observing environmental conditions to guide farming, livestock management and resource use.

◆ STRENGTHS OF INDIGENOUS PRACTICES
✓ Developed from long-term experience with local environments.
✓ Often use locally available resources.
✓ Can conserve biodiversity and natural resources.
✓ May require relatively low financial and technological inputs.
✓ Encourage community participation and responsibility.
✓ Can be well adapted to local climatic and ecological conditions.
✓ Help preserve local knowledge and cultural practices.

◆ LIMITATIONS AND CHALLENGES
✓ Some traditional practices may not be sufficient for today's population and environmental pressures.
✓ Population growth can increase pressure on traditional resource-management systems.
✓ Climate change may make some traditional practices less effective or predictable.
✓ Traditional knowledge may be lost when younger generations adopt different lifestyles.
✓ Some practices can have negative environmental effects if used in inappropriate conditions or at excessive levels.
✓ Modern environmental problems may require scientific knowledge, technology and larger-scale cooperation in addition to indigenous knowledge.

◆ USING INDIGENOUS KNOWLEDGE TODAY
Indigenous practices should not simply be rejected or adopted without assessment. Their strengths can be combined with appropriate modern science, technology and environmental policies.

The most effective approach is to recognize useful local knowledge, involve communities in environmental decision-making, test practices under current conditions, and combine traditional knowledge with modern scientific knowledge where appropriate.

title: KEY TERMS OF UNIT 6
notes:
Environmental problem → a condition that harms the natural environment or human well-being.

Environmental degradation → deterioration of the natural environment and its resources.

Ecological footprint → the biologically productive land and water area required to support a population's resource consumption and waste absorption.

Sustainability → the ability to maintain environmental, economic and social well-being over the long term.

Carrying capacity → the maximum population an environment can support sustainably.

Biocapacity → the capacity of ecosystems to regenerate biological resources and absorb certain wastes.

Renewable energy → energy obtained from sources that are naturally replenished.

Environmental education → education that develops knowledge, attitudes, skills and responsible action for environmental protection.

Environmental stewardship → responsible care and management of the environment.

Indigenous environmental knowledge → locally developed knowledge and practices concerning the environment and natural-resource management.
